title: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
blurb: Recognise neuroleptic malignant syndrome early, tell it apart from look-alikes and act: stop the antipsychotic and get urgent medical care.
question: Ms Burke, 41, takes olanzapine. Over two days she has become confused and sweaty, with a temperature of 39.4 °C, pulse 128, fluctuating blood pressure and stiff limbs. What is the most likely cause and the priority action?

teach.body: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a rare but potentially fatal reaction to antipsychotic drugs. The BNF describes hyperthermia, a fluctuating level of consciousness, muscle rigidity and autonomic dysfunction (fever, tachycardia, labile blood pressure, sweating); product information adds raised serum creatine kinase (CK). It can occur with any antipsychotic, old or new. In plain English: a hot, stiff, confused person with an unstable pulse and BP who is on an antipsychotic has NMS until proven otherwise.

teach.h: Scenario: Ms Burke on the rehabilitation ward
teach.body: Staff Nurse Adeyemi finds Ms Burke hot, sweaty, confused and stiff, with NEWS2 well above her baseline. Recognising possible NMS, she withholds the evening olanzapine, calls the duty doctor urgently and, as the unit has no acute medical cover overnight, arranges emergency transfer by 999. While waiting she repeats observations, removes heavy bedding, encourages fluids if safe and documents clearly. At the acute hospital, CK is raised and NMS is confirmed.

teach.text: Do not treat the confusion and agitation of NMS as worsening psychosis and give more antipsychotic, or rapid tranquillisation; that adds fuel. And 'she is on a newer drug, so it cannot be NMS' is wrong: NMS can occur with any antipsychotic.

teach.caption: BNF: discontinuation is essential for at least 5 days, preferably longer, and signs should resolve completely.

items: NMS: hyperthermia, rigidity, altered consciousness and autonomic instability; raised CK.
Rare, potentially fatal, possible with any antipsychotic.
Withhold the antipsychotic and escalate as a medical emergency; transfer to acute care if needed.
Distinguish from serotonin syndrome (hours, clonus, hyperreflexia) and dystonia (no fever).
Antipsychotic off for at least 5 days and until signs resolve; specialist decides any restart.

summary: You can now recognise the core features of neuroleptic malignant syndrome, separate it from serotonin syndrome and other look-alikes, and take the right immediate actions. You can also explain what happens to antipsychotic treatment afterwards.

A.q: Which group of features is characteristic of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
options: Hyperthermia, rigidity, confusion, unstable BP
Clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhoea, shivering
Coarse tremor, vomiting, ataxia, polyuria
Neck spasm, upward gaze, normal temperature
A.why: BNF: NMS presents with hyperthermia, fluctuating consciousness, muscle rigidity and autonomic dysfunction such as labile blood pressure.

whyNot.3: These describe acute dystonia with oculogyric crisis.

A.q: Which blood test result supports a diagnosis of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
options: Low serum sodium
Low prolactin level
Raised lithium level
Raised creatine kinase
A.why: Antipsychotic SPCs list increased serum creatine (phospho)kinase as a feature of NMS, reflecting muscle breakdown.

whyNot.0: Hyponatraemia is linked with SSRIs, not a marker of NMS.
whyNot.1: Antipsychotics usually raise prolactin, and prolactin does not diagnose NMS.
whyNot.2: A raised lithium level indicates lithium toxicity.

A.q: After an episode of NMS, how long does the BNF advise the antipsychotic should be stopped?
options: For at least 5 days and until resolved
For 24 hours, then restart at a lower dose
Until the next depot injection is due
For 48 hours if the CK is normal
A.why: BNF: discontinuation is essential for at least 5 days, preferably longer, and signs should resolve completely.

whyNot.2: Depot timing is irrelevant; the drug must be stopped.
whyNot.3: 48 hours is shorter than the BNF advice.

B.q: Ms Rowe, 37, takes aripiprazole. A colleague says she cannot develop NMS because it is a newer antipsychotic. Which reply is accurate?
options: Correct: NMS occurs with typical drugs
Correct: aripiprazole lowers NMS risk to zero
Incorrect: NMS can occur with any antipsychotic
Incorrect: NMS occurs with antidepressants too
B.why: BNF: NMS is a rare but potentially fatal side effect of all antipsychotic drugs, first- and second-generation.

whyNot.0: NMS is not limited to typical antipsychotics.
whyNot.1: No antipsychotic carries zero NMS risk.
whyNot.3: The serotonergic reaction to antidepressants is serotonin syndrome, a different condition.

B.q: Ms Field, 46, takes an antipsychotic and an SSRI. She is febrile, sweaty and confused. Which finding points towards NMS rather than serotonin syndrome?
options: Onset within hours of an SSRI increase
Clonus and brisk reflexes in the legs
Lead-pipe rigidity developing over days
Diarrhoea and shivering with tremor
B.why: NMS typically develops over days with generalised lead-pipe rigidity and reduced reflexes; serotonin syndrome is rapid with clonus and hyperreflexia.

whyNot.0: Rapid onset after a serotonergic change suggests serotonin syndrome.
whyNot.1: Clonus and hyperreflexia are typical of serotonin syndrome.
whyNot.3: Diarrhoea, shivering and tremor fit serotonin syndrome.

B.q: Mr Webb, 45, is transferred to an acute medical ward with NMS. Which nursing care is most important while he is treated?
options: Frequent observations, fluid balance and cooling
Restarting his antipsychotic at a lower dose
Restraint to prevent him leaving the bed
Daily weights and a low-fat diet plan
B.why: SPCs advise withdrawal of the antipsychotic with supportive therapy and careful monitoring: observations, fluid balance and temperature control.

whyNot.1: Antipsychotics stay off for at least 5 days and until NMS resolves.
whyNot.2: Restraint is not a treatment for NMS and adds physical strain.
whyNot.3: Weight and diet are not priorities in an acute emergency.

C.q: Ms Burke, 41, on olanzapine, has a temperature of 39.4 °C, pulse 128, fluctuating BP, stiff limbs and new confusion. Her evening dose is due. What should the nurse do first?
options: Give the dose, then repeat her observations
Give PRN haloperidol to settle her agitation
Withhold the dose and get urgent medical review
Offer paracetamol and recheck in 4 hours
C.why: These are the core features of NMS. The antipsychotic is withheld and the situation escalated as a medical emergency (BNF; SPCs).

whyNot.0: Giving more antipsychotic may worsen NMS.
whyNot.1: Another antipsychotic adds to the cause.
whyNot.3: A 4-hour delay is unsafe with this degree of physiological disturbance.

C.q: At 02:00 on a stand-alone mental health unit with no on-site medical team, Mr Lyle, 60, has suspected NMS with a temperature of 40 °C and reduced consciousness. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ask the on-call psychiatrist to review him in the morning
Call 999 for emergency transfer to an acute hospital
Give PRN lorazepam and start 15-minute observations
Start oral fluids and recheck at the next handover
C.why: Suspected NMS with high fever and reduced consciousness is a medical emergency needing acute hospital care; without on-site medical cover, emergency transfer is required.

whyNot.2: Sedation and observation alone do not provide the medical care he needs.
whyNot.3: Oral fluids are unsafe with reduced consciousness, and delay is dangerous.

C.q: Two days after rapid tranquillisation with IM haloperidol and promethazine, Jamal, 28, is drowsy and rigid with a temperature of 38.9 °C. What does this most likely require?
options: A further IM dose, as he is still unsettled
A sleep diary to assess his drowsiness
Seclusion until his behaviour settles
Urgent medical review for possible NMS
C.why: Fever, rigidity and altered consciousness after an antipsychotic suggest NMS; NG10 1.4.45 post-RT monitoring of temperature and consciousness is meant to catch such complications early.

whyNot.0: Another antipsychotic dose could worsen NMS.
whyNot.2: Seclusion does not address a medical emergency.

reteach.title: Hot, stiff, confused, unstable
reteach.question: What should make you think of NMS?

blocks.body: Hot (fever), stiff (rigidity), confused (altered consciousness) and unstable (pulse, BP, sweating) in anyone on an antipsychotic. Two actions follow: withhold the antipsychotic and escalate as a medical emergency. Raised CK supports the diagnosis.

blocks.text: NMS can happen with any antipsychotic, including newer ones.

explain.body: Hyperthermia, fluctuating consciousness, muscle rigidity and autonomic dysfunction (tachycardia, labile BP, sweating). Raised CK reflects muscle damage.

test.q: Which finding is one of the core features of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
options: Muscle rigidity
Galactorrhoea
Weight gain
Hypersalivation
test.why: Muscle rigidity is a core feature of NMS, with hyperthermia, altered consciousness and autonomic instability.

whyNot.2: Weight gain is a metabolic side effect.
whyNot.3: Hypersalivation is common with clozapine, not a core NMS feature.

explain.body: Withhold the antipsychotic, escalate as a medical emergency, monitor closely with NEWS2 and arrange acute medical care. Supportive care includes fluids and cooling as directed.

test.q: What is the first priority when NMS is suspected in a patient on an antipsychotic?
options: Reduce the antipsychotic dose by half
Switch to a different antipsychotic
Withhold it and escalate urgently
Give an antimuscarinic and observe
test.why: SPCs and BNF: the antipsychotic must be withdrawn, with urgent supportive treatment and monitoring.

whyNot.0: Any continued antipsychotic exposure risks worsening NMS.

explain.body: Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs within hours, with clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor and diarrhoea. NMS follows antipsychotics, usually over days, with lead-pipe rigidity and reduced reflexes.

test.q: Which feature most suggests serotonin syndrome rather than NMS?
options: Lead-pipe rigidity
Slow onset over several days
Reduced tendon reflexes
Inducible clonus
test.why: Clonus and hyperreflexia are neuromuscular hallmarks of serotonin toxicity (BNF).

whyNot.0: Lead-pipe rigidity is typical of NMS.

explain.body: Keep antipsychotics off for at least 5 days, preferably longer, until signs resolve completely. Any restart is a specialist decision. Record the reaction clearly so all services know.

test.q: Mr Ellis's NMS signs are improving 2 days after stopping his antipsychotic. When might restarting be considered?
options: Today, as his signs are clearly improving
Once his temperature has returned to normal
After at least 5 days with full resolution
When his next depot injection is due
test.why: BNF: discontinue for at least 5 days, preferably longer, and allow signs and symptoms to resolve completely.

whyNot.0: Two days is too soon and he has not fully recovered.
whyNot.1: Loss of fever alone is not full resolution.
whyNot.3: Depot timing does not determine safety to restart.
